{{Short description|Mathematical folklore}}
{{Multiple issues|{{Tone|date=August 2023|introductory section|talk=Re-work the Introduction}}
{{More footnotes|date=October 2023}}}}

In mathematics, an '''infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure''' is a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] defined on infinite-dimensional [[Normed vector space|normed vector spaces]], such as [[Banach space|Banach spaces]], which resembles the [[Lebesgue measure]] used in finite-dimensional spaces.

However, the traditional Lebesgue measure cannot be straightforwardly extended to all infinite-dimensional spaces due to a key limitation: any translation-invariant [[Borel measure]] on an infinite-dimensional [[separable space|separable]] Banach space must be either infinite for all sets or zero for all sets. Despite this, certain forms of infinite-dimensional Lebesgue-like measures can exist in specific contexts. These include locally compact spaces like the [[Hilbert cube]], which is compact, or scenarios where some typical properties of finite-dimensional Lebesgue measures are modified or omitted.

==Motivation==
The Lebesgue measure <math>\lambda</math> on the [[Euclidean space]] <math>\Reals^n</math> is [[Locally finite measure|locally finite]], [[Strictly positive measure|strictly positive]], and [[Translational symmetry|translation-invariant]]. That is:
* every point <math>x</math> in <math>\Reals^n</math> has an open neighborhood <math>N_x</math> with finite measure: <math>\lambda(N_x) < + \infty;</math>
* every non-empty open subset <math>U</math> of <math>\Reals^n</math> has positive measure: <math>\lambda(U) > 0;</math> and
* if <math>A</math> is any Lebesgue-measurable subset of <math>\Reals^n,</math> and <math>h</math> is a vector in <math>\Reals^n,</math> then all translates of <math>A</math> have the same measure:  <math>\lambda(A+h) = \lambda(A).</math>
Motivated by their geometrical significance, constructing measures satisfying the above set properties for infinite-dimensional spaces such as the  [[Lp space|<math>L^p</math> spaces]] or [[Path space (algebraic topology)|path spaces]] is still an open and active area of research.

==Non-existence theorem in separable Banach spaces==
Let <math>X</math> be an infinite-dimensional, [[Separable space|separable]] Banach space. Then, the only locally finite and translation invariant [[Borel measure]] <math>\mu</math> on <math>X</math> is a [[trivial measure]]. Equivalently, there is no locally finite, strictly positive, and translation invariant measure on <math>X</math>.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last=Oxtoby |first=John C. |date=1946 |title=Invariant measures in groups which are not locally compact |journal=Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. |volume=60 |pages=216 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1946-0018188-5}}</ref>

=== Statement for non locally compact Polish groups ===
More generally: on a non locally compact [[Polish group]] <math>G</math>, there cannot exist a [[Σ-finite measure|σ-finite]] and [[Left invariant|left-invariant]] Borel measure.<ref name=":0" />

This theorem implies that on an infinite dimensional separable Banach space (which cannot be [[Locally compact space|locally compact]]) a measure that perfectly matches the properties of a finite dimensional Lebesgue measure does not exist.

===Proof===

Let <math>X</math> be an infinite-dimensional, separable Banach space equipped with a locally finite translation-invariant measure <math>\mu</math>. To prove that <math>\mu</math> is the trivial measure, it is sufficient and necessary to show that <math>\mu(X) = 0.</math>

Like every separable [[metric space]], <math>X</math> is a [[Lindelöf space]], which means that every open cover of <math>X</math> has a countable subcover. It is, therefore, enough to show that there exists some open cover of <math>X</math> by null sets because by choosing a countable subcover, the [[Set function#countably subadditive|σ-subadditivity]] of <math>\mu</math> will imply that <math>\mu(X) = 0.</math>

Using local finiteness of the measure <math>\mu</math>, suppose that for some <math>r > 0,</math> the [[open ball]] <math>B(r)</math> of radius <math>r</math> has a finite <math>\mu</math>-measure. Since <math>X</math> is infinite-dimensional, by [[Riesz's lemma]] there is an infinite sequence of [[pairwise disjoint]] open balls <math>B_n(r/4),</math> <math>n \in \N</math>, of radius <math>r/4,</math> with all the smaller balls <math>B_n(r/4)</math> contained within <math>B(r).</math> By translation invariance, all the cover's balls have the same <math>\mu</math>-measure, and since the infinite sum of these finite <math>\mu</math>-measures are finite, the cover's balls must all have <math>\mu</math>-measure zero.

Since <math>r</math> was arbitrary, every open ball in <math>X</math> has zero <math>\mu</math>-measure, and taking a cover of <math>X</math> which is the set of all open balls that completes the proof that <math>\mu(X) = 0</math>.

==Nontrivial measures==
Here are some examples of infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measures that can exist if the conditions of the above theorem are relaxed.

One example for an entirely separable Banach space is the [[abstract Wiener space]] construction, similar to a product of Gaussian measures (which are not translation invariant). Another approach is to consider a Lebesgue measure of finite-dimensional subspaces within the larger space and look at [[prevalent and shy sets]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Hunt, Brian R. and Sauer, Tim and Yorke, James A.|title=Prevalence: a translation-invariant "almost every" on infinite-dimensional spaces|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.)|volume=27|year=1992|pages=217&ndash;238|doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-1992-00328-2|issue=2|arxiv=math/9210220|bibcode=1992math.....10220H|s2cid=17534021}}</ref>

The [[Hilbert cube]] carries the [[product measure|product Lebesgue measure]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Oxtoby |first1=John C. |last2=Prasad |first2=Vidhu S. |title=Homeomorphic Measures on the Hilbert Cube |journal=Pacific J. Math. |date=1978 |volume=77 |issue=2 |pages=483–497 |doi=10.2140/pjm.1978.77.483 |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/pacific-journal-of-mathematics/volume-77/issue-2/Homeomorphic-measures-in-the-Hilbert-cube/pjm/1102806462.full}}</ref> and the compact [[topological group]] given by the [[Tychonoff product]] of an infinite number of copies of the [[circle group]] is infinite-dimensional and carries a [[Haar measure]] that is translation-invariant. These two spaces can be mapped onto each other in a measure-preserving way by unwrapping the circles into intervals. The infinite product of the additive real numbers has the analogous product Haar measure, which is precisely the infinite-dimensional analog of the Lebesgue measure.{{citation needed|date=January 2024}}
